text: If you've written circuit.inverse() or gate.control(1) in Qiskit, you've already used the ideas behind this lesson — but those are library methods that build a new circuit object by composing gates together. In Q#, give me the inverse and give me a controlled version are language-level functors: the compiler derives them automatically from how you wrote the original operation.

A functor takes an operation and produces a related one without you writing new code. Adjoint produces the inverse, undoing an operation's effect. Controlled produces a version that only executes if a set of control qubits are all |1>. You opt in by declaring is Adj + Ctl on your operation. This is a compiler guarantee in Q#, not a library-level convenience the way it is in Qiskit — and not every operation qualifies. Something that isn't reversible, like a measurement, simply can't be adjointed.

PrepareSuperposition is declared is Adj + Ctl, so you can call it normally, call Adjoint PrepareSuperposition to undo it, or call Controlled PrepareSuperposition with an array of control qubits to apply it conditionally. For a simple self-inverse gate like H, the compiler works out that H is its own inverse — you never write that logic yourself.

Functors compose with operations that do more than one gate's worth of work. EncodeAngle applies Ry then S. Notice the order reversal in the generated adjoint: to undo Ry then S, the compiler doesn't just invert each gate in the original order — it reverses the sequence and inverts each step, giving undo S, then undo Ry. That's exactly the mathematically correct way to invert a composed sequence of unitary operations, and it's exactly what you'd have to work out by hand building this as a Qiskit circuit method yourself.

Qiskit's inverse and control methods operate on already-built circuit objects — nothing in its type system requires every gate to support them correctly by construction; that's on you. In Q#, is Adj plus Ctl is a declaration the compiler checks: if your operation's body contains something that can't be adjointed or controlled — a measurement, which is not unitary and has no well-defined inverse — the compiler rejects the claim at compile time, rather than letting you discover the problem at runtime.
Next lesson's lab pulls everything from this chapter together: a reusable state-preparation operation you write yourself, undone by its own compiler-generated Adjoint, and verified by measurement.
